facts.fact: Opened on 9 May 2015 at Largo Isarco as the Fondazione's new permanent Milan venue.
facts.quote: On 9 May 2015, the Fondazione Prada unveiled its new permanent Milan venue, in Largo Isarco.

facts.fact: OMA, led by Rem Koolhaas, conceived the venue.
facts.quote: The new Milan venue of the Fondazione, conceived by architecture firm OMA—led by Rem Koolhaas—expands the repertoire of spatial typologies in which art can be exhibited and shared with the public.

facts.fact: It transforms a former distillery from the 1910s, adding three new structures to the existing buildings.
facts.quote: The complex, which is the result of the transformation of a former distillery dating back to the 1910s, is articulated by an architectural configuration which combines preexisting buildings with three new structures, named “Podium”, “Cinema” and “Torre”.

facts.fact: The "Haunted House" is a four-storey building clad in gold foil that displays the permanent collection.
facts.quote: The hallmark of the new venue is the so-called “Haunted House”, a 4-story building, clad in 24 carat gold foil, where pieces from the permanent collection of art of the Fondazione Prada are permanently on display.

facts.fact: The film director Wes Anderson recreated the mood of old Milan cafés in the bar.
facts.quote: The entrance building welcomes visitors to two new facilities, developed through special collaborations: a kids' area designed by a group of students from the École nationale supérieure d'architecture de Versailles, and a bar where director Wes Anderson has recreated the typical mood of old Milan cafés.

facts.fact: Sultan Bayezid I commissioned it to mark his victory at the Battle of Nicopolis; it was built 1396–1399.
facts.quote: It was commissioned by the Ottoman Sultan Bayezid I to commemorate his great victory at the Battle of Nicopolis and built between 1396 and 1399.

facts.fact: It is a major monument of early Ottoman architecture in the old city beside the historic markets.
facts.quote: The mosque is a major monument of early Ottoman architecture and one of the most important mosques in the city, located in the heart of the old city alongside its historic markets.

facts.fact: Ali Neccar designed and built it.
facts.quote: Ordered by Sultan Bayezid I, the mosque was designed and built by architect Ali Neccar in 1396–1399.

facts.fact: Twenty domes in four rows of five sit on twelve columns.
facts.quote: Its interior space is covered by twenty domes arranged in four rows of five that are supported by twelve columns.

facts.fact: Tradition says the twenty domes stand in place of twenty separate mosques the Sultan had promised.
facts.quote: A popular tradition holds that Sultan Bayezid I built a mosque of twenty domes instead of building twenty separate mosques which he had promised in return for winning the Battle of Nicopolis in 1396.

facts.fact: A fountain under a dome open to the sky (now glazed) lights the interior and served ablutions.
facts.quote: The dome over the şadırvan is open to the sky (though covered by glass today), creating a skylight which helps to illuminate the mosque's dark interior.

facts.fact: It has three entrances, the northern one the most monumental.
facts.quote: It has three entrances (to the north, west and east), of which the northern entrance is the most monumental.

facts.fact: An earthquake in 1855 collapsed the roof and closed the mosque for years.
facts.quote: Following a damaging earthquake in 1855 which caused the roof to collapse, the mosque was closed for a number of years.

facts.fact: It is a passenger terminal for the annual Hajj pilgrimage at Jeddah's King Abdulaziz International Airport.
facts.quote: The Hajj Terminal is a passenger terminal dedicated to the annual Haji pilgrimage at King Abdulaziz International Airport, the principal airport serving Jeddah and Mecca, Saudi Arabia.

facts.fact: SOM won the design contract in 1975.
facts.quote: International architecture and engineering firm Skidmore, Owings & Merrill won the contract for designing the terminal in 1975.

facts.fact: The architects based the design on traditional Bedouin tents rather than a standard enclosed building.
facts.quote: Instead of constructing a standard, enclosed building for the airport which would not reflect the kingdom's culture, the architects based it off traditional Bedouin tents.

facts.fact: Fazlur Khan said the main terminal space should be an open, shaded space.
facts.quote: We felt that from a local and cultural viewpoint, the main terminal space should be an open, shaded space.

facts.fact: The roof uses a translucent fibre sheet developed by Owens-Corning.
facts.quote: A translucent material developed by Owens-Corning produced a thin fibre sheet for the roof.

facts.fact: A terminal with permanent tents was unheard of at the time.
facts.quote: At the time, a terminal permanently incorporating tents was unheard of.

facts.fact: Hochtief was general contractor.
facts.quote: West German engineering firm, Hochtief was entrusted as the general contractor for the project.

facts.fact: Construction began in 1979 and finished in 1982 (the article's infobox gives an inauguration date of 31 May 1981).
facts.quote: Construction began in 1979, and was completed within a three-year timeframe in 1982.

facts.fact: It is in Hijiyama Park, Hiroshima.
facts.quote: It is in Hijiyama Park in Hiroshima, Japan.

facts.fact: Kisho Kurokawa designed the building.
facts.quote: The building was designed by architect Kisho Kurokawa.

facts.fact: It was the first public contemporary art museum to open in Japan.
facts.quote: It was the first public contemporary art museum to open in Japan, and its exhibitions focus on post-1945, contemporary emerging artists and artworks that link contemporary art with Hiroshima.

facts.fact: The museum was founded in 1989.
facts.quote: The Hiroshima City Museum of Contemporary Art (広島市現代美術館, Hiroshima-shi Gendai Bijutsukan) is an art museum founded in 1989.

facts.fact: It is a centre for the performing arts in Jerusalem.
facts.quote: The Jerusalem Theatre (Hebrew: תיאטרון ירושלים, a.k.a. The Jerusalem Centre for the Performing Arts) is a centre for the performing arts in Jerusalem.

facts.fact: A 1958 municipal design competition was won by Michael Nadler, Shulamit Nadler and Shmuel Bixson.
facts.quote: Architects Michael Nadler, Shulamit Nadler and Shmuel Bixson won first prize.

facts.fact: The complex has four performance halls of different sizes.
facts.quote: The complex consists of the Sherover Theatre, which seats 950, the Henry Crown Symphony Hall (home of the Jerusalem Symphony Orchestra) with 750 seats, the Rebecca Crown Auditorium, with 450 seats, and the Little Theatre with 110 seats.

facts.fact: Exposed concrete is combined with Jerusalem stone.
facts.quote: The theatre combines sculptural elements of exposed concrete with traditional Jerusalem stone construction.

facts.fact: It stands in a large public square used for outdoor events.
facts.quote: It sits in a large public square that is used for outdoor concerts and other events.

facts.fact: The Crown wing was designed by the same firm as a continuation of the original.
facts.quote: The planning and design of the new wing was carried out by the same architectural firm, so that the new wing, named for Crown's parents, was a natural continuation of the original design.

facts.fact: The building was dedicated in October 1971.
facts.quote: The building was dedicated in October 1971.

facts.fact: It was listed for preservation in 2012.
facts.quote: In 2012, the Jerusalem Theatre complex, together with the nearby Presidential Residence and the Van Leer Institute, was officially listed for historical preservation by the Jerusalem Municipality, reflecting its architectural and cultural significance in the city’s modern built environment.

facts.fact: It is an Edwardian building completed in 1914.
facts.quote: Johannesburg City Hall is an Edwardian building constructed in 1914 by the Hawkey and McKinley construction company.

facts.fact: A 1909 competition was open only to South African resident architects and judged by Leonard Stokes.
facts.quote: Only South African resident architects were allowed to take part and entries were judged by Leonard Stokes, Vice-President of the Royal Institute of British Architects and a decision was made in March 1910.

facts.fact: A Cape Town firm won the competition; a different man, Mattheus Meischke, won the building contract.
facts.quote: A Cape Town architectural firm, Hawke and McKinlay, won the competition to design the new building but it took until 17 February 1912 before Mattheus Meischke was awarded the tender to construct the building which would cost £503,000.

facts.fact: The style is Edwardian Baroque with an Ionic portico and a neo-Renaissance tower.
facts.quote: The style is described as Edwardian Baroque with a portico of Ionic columns and tower with a half dome entrance described as neo-Renaissance.

facts.fact: It has two halves: municipal offices to the east, the Town Hall to the west.
facts.quote: The building is designed as two-halves, with the eastern side consisting of the municipal offices which faces Rissik Street and the western side containing the Town Hall facing Harrison Street.

facts.fact: In 1937 the tower was taken down, a floor added, and the tower rebuilt.
facts.quote: In 1937, the City Hall would undergo further construction when the tower was dismantled and an additional floor was added to the building and then the tower rebuilt.

facts.fact: It became a National Monument in 1979.
facts.quote: On 12 October 1979, City Hall was designated a National Monument.

facts.fact: The Gauteng Provincial Legislature moved in during 1995.
facts.quote: After the 1994 South African elections, the Gauteng Provincial Legislature moved from Pretoria to Johannesburg and on 21 October 1995 the City Hall would become its new home.

facts.fact: It is a pedestrian shopping street designed by Jo van den Broek and Jaap Bakema to rebuild Rotterdam after the 1940 bombing; it opened 9 October 1953.
facts.quote: It was designed by Jo van den Broek and Jaap Bakema as part of the rebuilding of the city after the German bombing of 1940, and opened on 9 October 1953.

facts.fact: It has been described as the first purpose-built pedestrian street in Europe.
facts.quote: It has been described as the first purpose-built pedestrian street in Europe.

facts.fact: Shops face a car-free promenade, are serviced from streets behind, and housing sits in separate blocks.
facts.quote: The design separated the functions that had shared the pre-war streets. Shops lined a car-free promenade and were supplied from service streets behind them, while housing went into separate apartment blocks.

facts.fact: A 1:100 model won over the sceptical shopkeepers.
facts.quote: The 66 shopkeepers taking part were sceptical at first, but a model at 1:100 scale won them over.

facts.fact: Lewis Mumford praised it in 1957.
facts.quote: The American critic Lewis Mumford praised it in The New Yorker in 1957.

facts.fact: It was cited as a model abroad, such as Stevenage town centre.
facts.quote: The street has also been cited as a model for pedestrian shopping areas abroad, such as the town centre of Stevenage.

facts.fact: The original section became a national monument in 2010.
facts.quote: The original section has been a rijksmonument (national monument) since 2010.

facts.fact: The name refers to ropewalks once in the area.
facts.quote: They also objected to the name, which refers to the ropewalks once located in the area, and would have preferred to call the street the Promenade.

facts.fact: It is a high-speed station in Reggio Emilia on the Milan–Bologna line.
facts.quote: The station is located on the Milan–Bologna high-speed railway and Reggio Emilia-Guastalla railway.

facts.fact: A regional line has linked it to central Reggio Emilia since December 2013.
facts.quote: Since 15 December 2013 the station has been connected to the regional line Reggio Emilia-Guastalla railway, offering a connection to the centre of Reggio Emilia.

facts.fact: Lev Rudnev designed it; it is the tallest of Moscow's Stalinist "Seven Sisters" (1947–1953).
facts.quote: It was designed by Lev Rudnev as the headquarters of Moscow State University,  and is the tallest among the "Seven Sisters" constructed in Moscow between 1947 and 1953 in the Stalinist architectural style.

facts.fact: It was the tallest building in Europe from 1953 to 1990.
facts.quote: It was the tallest building in Europe for 37 years, from 1953 to 1990,  before being surpassed by the Messeturm in Germany.

facts.fact: Lower lateral towers and dormitory wings enclose a cour d'honneur courtyard with the central tower.
facts.quote: Lateral towers are lower than the central one; two 18 and 9 storey dormitory wings define, with the central corpus of the complex, a cour d'honneur courtyard.

facts.fact: Boris Iofan lost the commission after placing his draft on the edge of Sparrow Hills, a landslide-prone site.
facts.quote: The leading architect Boris Iofan bid for the skyscraper project in 1947 but the job was assigned to Lev Rudnev, because Iofan made a mistake placing his draft skyscraper right on the edge of Sparrow Hills, a site concerned with a potential landslide hazard.

facts.fact: Rudnev set the building back from the cliff.
facts.quote: He set the building 800 meters away from the cliff.

facts.fact: The tower was inaugurated on 1 September 1953 and has a steel framework.
facts.quote: The main tower, which consumed over 40,000 tons of steel for its framework and 130,000 cubic metres of concrete, was inaugurated on September 1, 1953.

facts.fact: Sculptures decorate the building, including a student couple by Vera Mukhina.
facts.quote: Among the statues which decorate the building is a sculpture by Vera Mukhina representing a couple of students and a statue by N. Tomsky of Mikhail Lomonosov (1711–1765), the founder of Moscow University.

facts.fact: The skyline inspired buildings such as Warsaw's Palace of Culture and Science.
facts.quote: The University skyline inspired various buildings in the socialist countries, like the Palace of Culture and Science in Warsaw, and also the logo of 1980 Moscow Olympic Games.

facts.fact: It is Singapore's flagship national library, in twin 16-storey blocks linked by bridges on the upper floors.
facts.quote: A subsidiary of the National Library Board (NLB), it consists of twin 16-storey blocks, linked by bridges on the upper floors, with three underground basements

facts.fact: It replaced the old National Library at Stamford Road, which closed in March 2004.
facts.quote: The current building, a 16-storey, two-block development situated in the city's Civic District, replaces the old National Library at Stamford Road, which closed on 31 March 2004.

facts.fact: Ken Yeang's firm T.R. Hamzah & Yeang won the design contract after he split from the first design team.
facts.quote: Ken Yeang co-founded a Malaysian architectural firm T.R. Hamzah & Yeang   based in Kuala Lumpur and the new firm was awarded the design contract for the National Library by the Ministry of National Development.

facts.fact: It was officially opened on 12 November 2005.
facts.quote: The library moved to its new home on 22 July 2005, and the building was officially opened on 12 November that year by the then-President S. R. Nathan.

facts.fact: A reference library and a public library share the building.
facts.quote: It is the flagship building of the National Library Board, bringing together the core functions of the old library by incorporating a reference library, known as the Lee Kong Chian Reference Library (simplified Chinese: 李光前参考图书馆; traditional Chinese: 李光前參考圖書館; pinyin: Lǐguāngqián cānkǎo túshū guǎn), as well as a public library, the Central Public Library, under one roof.

facts.fact: A large bubble-like room called The Pod sits on the top level.
facts.quote: On the highest 16th level rooftop, there is a large closed area designed like a bubble called The Pod, used for functions and events.

facts.fact: Old bricks from the earlier library were reused.
facts.quote: A number of old bricks from the old National Library building has been incorporated into the present building.

facts.fact: The courthouse was first proposed in 1925 to replace seven small judicial offices.
facts.quote: The concept of constructing a new courthouse in Porta Vittoria to replace the seven small and outdated judicial offices then existing in Milan was initially proposed in 1925.

facts.fact: Marcello Piacentini, with Ernesto Rapisardi, designed it; it was finished in July 1940.
facts.quote: In collaboration with architect Ernesto Rapisardi, Piacentini designed and supervised the construction of the new courthouse, which was ultimated in July 1940.

facts.fact: One building holds three judicial institutions.
facts.quote: The building is an imposing structure situated on a centrally located site, conceived as a unified edifice housing three distinct judicial institutions: the Court of Appeal (Corte d'Appello), the Court (Tribunale), and the Magistrates Court (Pretura).

facts.fact: A tower stands at the southwest corner.
facts.quote: At the southwest corner stands a tower rising 61 meters high, originally intended to house the Archive.

facts.fact: It is mainly reinforced concrete with stone and marble decoration inside.
facts.quote: Constructed predominantly with reinforced concrete, the courthouse's interior features decorative elements crafted from precious stones and marble.

facts.fact: The exterior is austere while the interior is richly decorated.
facts.quote: While the exterior of the building presents a restrained and somewhat austere appearance, the interior is richly adorned with artistic embellishments, including bas-reliefs, mosaics, frescoes, and sculptures.

facts.fact: Artists including Mario Sironi and Fausto Melotti made the decoration.
facts.quote: These decorative works were realized by various prominent artists, notably Mario Sironi, Fausto Melotti, Carlo Carrà, Romano Romanelli, Achille Funi, and Arturo Dazzi.

facts.fact: The 2,400-seat hall by Jean Nouvel is the core of a complex in Parc de la Villette; it opened in January 2015.
facts.quote: At the core of this set of spaces is the symphonic concert hall of 2,400 seats designed by Jean Nouvel and opened in January 2015.

facts.fact: Its construction was postponed about twenty years to finish the Cité de la Musique first.
facts.quote: Its construction had been postponed for about twenty years to complete the current musical institution la Cité de la Musique designed by Christian de Portzamparc and opened in 1995.

facts.fact: Nouvel won the design competition in April 2007.
facts.quote: The renowned French architect Jean Nouvel won the design competition for the building in April 2007.

facts.fact: Nouvel worked with acousticians and a scenographer.
facts.quote: He brought in Brigitte Métra as his partner, along with Marshall Day Acoustics (room acoustics design) and Nagata Acoustics (peer-review and scale model study) and dUCKS Scéno (scenography).

facts.fact: Floating balconies keep the farthest listener close to the conductor.
facts.quote: The acoustic and architectural characteristics of the main concert hall have been described as "retaining a real sense of intimacy" which is "achieved by various floating balconies that enable even the farthest spectator to be only 36 yards away from the conductor."

facts.fact: A rooftop Belvedere has a path winding down to the park.
facts.quote: From the Belvedere on the roof where the Eiffel Tower can be seen a path snakes downward to the park.

facts.fact: Nouvel missed the opening concert amid a dispute over cost and completion date.
facts.quote: The opening concert was attended by French President François Hollande, the President of France  but not by Jean Nouvel, because of an ongoing dispute about the final costs and date of the building's completion.

facts.fact: It is a public art museum on the South Saskatchewan River in Saskatoon.
facts.quote: The art museum is situated along the west bank of the South Saskatchewan River, at the River Landing development in Saskatoon's Central Business District.

facts.fact: Bruce Kuwabara of KPMB Architects designed it with Architecture49.
facts.quote: The museum's 11,582 square metres (124,670 sq ft) building was designed by Bruce Kuwabara of KPMB Architects in association with Architecture49.

facts.fact: Construction ran from June 2013 and it opened in October 2017.
facts.quote: Construction for the art museum took place from June 2013 to 2017, and was opened to the public in October 2017.

facts.fact: The design draws on Prairie style and the region's barns, sheds and silos.
facts.quote: The building's design is influenced by Frank Lloyd Wright's Prairie style. The design of the building's exterior was based on region's open prairie landscape, and the barns, field sheds, and silos that occupy that space.

facts.fact: Cantilevered stacks extend toward the river and the skin is glass and copper mesh.
facts.quote: The exterior features cantilevered stacks that extend towards the South Saskatchewan River; and its glass and copper mesh exterior.

facts.fact: The steel mesh is a solar shading device.
facts.quote: The exterior steel mesh is a solar shading device and provides a shadowing effect on the building as the sun arcs through the sky.

facts.fact: The atrium rises to the fourth level with glass walls overlooking the river.
facts.quote: The "openness" of the prairie landscape were also reflected in the interior design of the building, with the ceiling of the main atrium extending to the fourth level of the building, and its walls being made of glass and overlooking the South Saskatchewan River.

facts.fact: It is the current meeting place of Thailand's National Assembly, on the Chao Phraya River in Bangkok.
facts.quote: It is located in Bangkok on the east bank of the Chao Phraya River in Kiakkai neighbourhood of the Dusit District.

facts.fact: A team led by Theerapol Niyom won the design competition.
facts.quote: Sappaya-Sapasathan was designed by a team led by Theerapol Niyom, who was the winner in the building's design competition.

facts.fact: Its main features include a central Thai pagoda, two chambers named for the Sun and the Moon, and teak.
facts.quote: Its main features are a Thai pagoda in the center of the building, Surya Hall (Hall of the Sun) for House of Representative, Chandra Hall (Hall of the Moon) for Senate of Thailand, and the use of 5,018 teak trees as they represent the "DNA of Thailand".

facts.fact: The design was inspired by a Thai Buddhist tale and made to look like a temple.
facts.quote: The building's design was inspired by a classic Thai Buddhist tale, Trai Bhum Phra Ruang, and was made to look like a temple as a reminder to officials of "Thainess" and morality, making it truly a Sappaya Sapasathan, "peaceful parliament".

facts.fact: It also houses museums, a convention center and offices.
facts.quote: It also houses museums, a convention center, a seminar room, a banquet hall, and offices.

facts.fact: The design has been criticised as "religious architecture".
facts.quote: The design has been criticised for being "religious architecture", embracing "elements of Buddhist and Hindu cosmology".

facts.fact: It opened officially on 1 May 2021 after delays and a budget rise.
facts.quote: The building was officially opened on 1 May 2021 after significant delays.

facts.fact: Philip Johnson designed it; it is made of Italian travertine with a grand hall and a distinctive central staircase.
facts.quote: The building, designed by architect Philip Johnson and funded by siblings Mary Frances and Adams Bromley Sheldon, is made of Italian travertine, featuring a grand hall and distinctive central staircase.

facts.fact: It was the dedicated home for the university's art collection from 1963.
facts.quote: The museum was established in 1963 when the university's art collection was moved to dedicated building at 451 North 12th Street.

facts.fact: The great hall has a suspended grand staircase.
facts.quote: The building, constructed of Italian travertine, includes an ornate great hall and a suspended grand staircase.

facts.fact: Isamu Noguchi made a work for the grand hall for the opening.
facts.quote: Japanese-American sculptor Isamu Noguchi was invited to create and install a work in the grand hall, which he titled "Song of the Bird," as part of the building's opening ceremonies.

facts.fact: Johnson called it the best building he ever designed.
facts.quote: Architect Philip Johnson proclaimed the Sheldon the best building he ever designed

facts.fact: It was designed to avoid "museum fatigue".
facts.quote: The building was designed to avoid what Johnson called "museum fatigue," a state of physical or mental exhaustion common among museum patrons.

facts.fact: The Sheldon siblings funded the project.
facts.quote: The siblings funded the entire project, combining to give over $1.5 million.

facts.fact: It was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 2013.
facts.quote: It was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 2013.

facts.fact: It is a mausoleum in Mashhad, designed by Hooshang Seyhoun and completed in 1963.
facts.quote: Designed by Hooshang Seyhoun and completed in 1963, the structure contains the grave of Nader Shah.

facts.fact: It was added to Iran's National Heritage List in 1975.
facts.quote: The structure was added to the Iran National Heritage List on 9 December 1975, administered by the Cultural Heritage, Handicrafts and Tourism Organization of Iran.

facts.fact: Nader Shah's body went uncommemorated until the 1960s.
facts.quote: Nader Shah's body remained un-commemorated until the 1960s when a concrete monument was constructed for him in the vicinity of a heavily polluted traffic intersection in Mashhad.

facts.fact: Nader Shah had ordered Mughal architects to build the Sun Palace as a jewel store and possible mausoleum.
facts.quote: Nader ordered the Mughal architects he had brought with himself to build the Sun Palace to store the jewels and possibly act as a mausoleum for him.

facts.fact: Gordon Bunshaft of SOM designed it.
facts.quote: It was designed by the prominent New York architect Gordon Bunshaft of the architectural firm Skidmore, Owings & Merrill LLP.

facts.fact: It was completed in 1965 as the company headquarters and still serves that purpose.
facts.quote: It was completed in 1965 for the insurance company's headquarters and it continues to serve that purpose.

facts.fact: The east and west walls have no windows; north and south windows admit daylight and keep out radiant heat.
facts.quote: The Modernist building has no windows on its east and west elevations. The windows on the north and south elevations allow in daylight and keep out radiant heat.

facts.fact: It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 2015.
facts.quote: It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 2015.

facts.fact: It is the oldest performing-arts school in modern Greece, founded in 1871.
facts.quote: The Athens Conservatoire (Greek: Ωδείον Αθηνών, romanized: Odeíon Athinón) is the oldest educational institution for the performing arts in modern Greece.

facts.fact: Ioannis Despotopoulos, who studied under Walter Gropius, designed the building.
facts.quote: Designed by the Greek architect Ioannis Despotopoulos (also known as Jan Despo), the only Greek to have studied under Bauhaus school founder Walter Gropius, the Conservatoire is the only completed part of an ambitious large-scale cultural complex commissioned in 1959 by the then government for Athens, for which he earned the top architectural prize of its time.

facts.fact: It is described as an example of Bauhaus and the modern movement in Greece.
facts.quote: It is an exceptional example of the Bauhaus school and the modern movement in Greece.

facts.fact: Building began in 1969 and stopped in 1976 for lack of funds.
facts.quote: The construction begun in 1969 and stopped in 1976, due to a lack of funding, leaving the building unfinished.

facts.fact: The state paid for completion in 1980 in exchange for the old headquarters.
facts.quote: In 1980, the Greek state undertook the cost of completing the work in exchange for ownership of the conservatory's old headquarters on Pireos Street.

facts.fact: Despotopoulos's wider plan included an opera house and a National Gallery extension, but only the Conservatoire was built.
facts.quote: According to Despotopoulos' archives on file at the Modern Greek Architecture section of the Benaki Museum, in addition to the Athens Conservatoire, his plan foresaw the construction of an 1,800-seat opera house, a circular theatre stage, an extension to the National Gallery, a new Byzantine Museum, a Byzantine-style church, a hotel, a hall for classical dance performances and the state orchestra, a playhouse for experimental theater, underground garages and more.

facts.fact: Underground floors housed the National Museum of Contemporary Art from 2008 to 2015.
facts.quote: A large part of the underground floors of the building was used to host the National Museum of Contemporary Art, Athens (EMST), between September 2008 and May 2015.

facts.fact: It is the largest public museum in Bahrain, in Manama, and opened 15 December 1988.
facts.quote: Opened on 15 December 1988 by the Emir of Bahrain Isa bin Salman Al Khalifa, the $30 million museum complex covers 27,800 sq meters and is the country's most popular tourist attraction.

facts.fact: It is considered the region's first modern museum.
facts.quote: It is widely considered to be the region's first modern museum.

facts.fact: Danish architects Krohn & Hartvig Rasmussen designed it.
facts.quote: The modern museum was designed by Danish architects Krohn & Hartvig Rasmussen and officially opened in December 1988.

facts.fact: It stands on an artificial peninsula overlooking Muharraq.
facts.quote: It was constructed on an artificial peninsula overlooking the neighbouring island of Muharraq.

facts.fact: It has two buildings and six permanent exhibitions.
facts.quote: The museum is made of two buildings spanning a floor space of 20,000 square meters.

facts.fact: A UNESCO agreement in 1967 helped pave the way for a national museum.
facts.quote: In 1967, a cultural agreement was signed between UNESCO and the Bahraini government which helped pave the way for the construction of a national museum.

facts.fact: Konstantin Melnikov designed it in 1926 with Vladimir Shukhov as structural engineer; completed 1927.
facts.quote: Bakhmetevsky Bus Garage was a public bus garage in Moscow, designed in 1926 by Konstantin Melnikov (floorplan concept and architectural design) and Vladimir Shukhov (structural engineering).

facts.fact: It applied avant-garde methods to an industrial building.
facts.quote: The building, completed in 1927, was an example of applying avant-garde architectural methods to an industrial facility.

facts.fact: Melnikov sold the city on a free-flow garage layout.
facts.quote: He approached city transportation board and sold his idea for a free-flow garage.

facts.fact: It is red-brick industrial in look; circular attic windows are its only avant-garde feature.
facts.quote: Bakhmetevsky Garage, sometimes associated with constructivist architecture, was in fact styled in an indefinite red-brick industrial livery; circular windows in the attic are the only avant-garde features (and even these were destroyed decades ago).

facts.fact: A parallelogram-shaped garage sits on a rectangular lot, with workshops and offices filling the gaps.
facts.quote: Melnikov also designed workshops and office buildings on the same lot, filling the irregular voids made by placing a parallelogram-shaped garage on a larger, rectangular lot.

facts.fact: It was restored in 2007–2008 and reopened as a modern art gallery.
facts.quote: Neglected for decades and nearly condemned to demolition, it was restored in 2007–2008 and reopened in September 2008 as a gallery of modern art.

facts.fact: It is a preserved coal-fired power station on the south bank of the Thames.
facts.quote: Battersea Power Station is a preserved coal-fired power station located on the south bank of the River Thames in Nine Elms in the London Borough of Wandsworth.

facts.fact: J. Theo Halliday and Giles Gilbert Scott were the architects.
facts.quote: The architects were J. Theo Halliday and Giles Gilbert Scott.

facts.fact: It is one of the world's largest brick buildings with Art Deco interior fittings.
facts.quote: The station is one of the world's largest brick buildings and notable for its original, Art Deco interior fittings and decor.

facts.fact: It was built in two stages with a near-identical design, giving four chimneys.
facts.quote: Battersea B was built to a design nearly identical to that of Battersea A, creating the iconic four-chimney structure.

facts.fact: A was built 1929–1935 and B 1937–1941, completed in 1955.

facts.fact: Philip Johnson was chosen after a lengthy global search.
facts.quote: After a lengthy global search, Peter Stewart, a Dallas businessman and one of the founders of the Thanks-Giving Foundation, chose architect Philip Johnson to design the project.

facts.fact: The square is set below ground level behind a wall, with fountains masking city noise.
facts.quote: The Square is set fifteen feet below ground level with a four-foot wall blocking the sight of automobiles to create a serene, green island. Water plays a prominent role in the landscape, with active fountains masking city noise.

facts.fact: Religious symbolism is intentionally absent from the decoration.
facts.quote: Overt religious symbolism is intentionally absent from the decoration of Thanks-Giving Square.

facts.fact: The Chapel of Thanksgiving is a spiral rising above street level.
facts.quote: The spiraling shape rises 90 feet (27.5 m) above street level, suggesting the infinite upward reach of the human spirit.

facts.fact: The chapel draws on the Great Mosque in Samarra.
facts.quote: The chapel's design takes its inspiration from the Great Mosque in Samarra, Iraq (itself derived from the square, spiral Pillar of Gor in Iran ) and the ancient spiral of life.

facts.fact: The chapel is entered across a bridge over a waterfall.
facts.quote: The entrance to the chapel is at the end of a 125-foot (38 m) bridge that runs over a cascading waterfall.

facts.fact: It hosted the 1922 Week of Modern Art and is a São Paulo landmark.
facts.quote: It is regarded as one of the landmarks of the city, significant both for its architectural value as well as for its historical importance, having been the venue for the Week of Modern Art in 1922, which revolutionised the arts in Brazil.

facts.fact: Ramos de Azevedo and the Italian architects Cláudio and Domiziano Rossi built it.
facts.quote: Ramos de Azevedo was the engineer assigned to the construction. He was also helped by two Italian architects Cláudio Rossi and Domiziano Rossi.

facts.fact: The architecture was inspired by the Palais Garnier, with most materials imported from Europe.
facts.quote: As was customary at the time, the majority of the construction materials was imported from Europe, and the architecture was inspired by the Palais Garnier of Paris.

facts.fact: Construction began in 1903 and lasted about 8 years.
facts.quote: The construction lasted about 8 years.

facts.fact: It stands on Morro do Chá (Tea Hill).
facts.quote: The place which was chosen for the construction was Morro do Chá, or Tea Hill, which had been the site of the new São José Theater.

facts.fact: The aristocracy wanted a theatre suited to large opera productions.
facts.quote: The aristocrats of the São Paulo demanded the creation of a new theatre, with a structure similar to some of the best theatres in the world and suitable for staging large opera productions.

facts.fact: It is a private music school in Chōfu, Tokyo.
facts.quote: Toho Gakuen School of Music (桐朋学園大学, Tōhō Gakuen Daigaku) is a private music school in Chōfu, Tokyo, Japan.

facts.fact: It displays the almost fully intact 17th-century warship Vasa on Djurgården and opened in 1990.
facts.quote: Located on the island of Djurgården, the museum displays the only almost fully intact 17th-century ship that has ever been salvaged, the 64-gun warship Vasa that sank on her maiden voyage in 1628. The Vasa Museum opened in 1990.

facts.fact: A 1981 competition drew 384 entries; Marianne Dahlbäck and Göran Månsson won with "Ask" (box).
facts.quote: A total of 384 architects sent in models of their ideas and the final winners were Marianne Dahlbäck and Göran Månsson with Ask ("box").

facts.fact: It was built around the old naval dry dock.
facts.quote: The construction of the new building began on and around the dry dock of the old naval yard with an inauguration ceremony hosted by Prince Bertil on 2 November 1987.

facts.fact: A large copper roof has stylised masts at the height of Vasa when fully rigged.
facts.quote: The new museum is dominated by a large copper roof with stylized masts that represent the actual height of Vasa when she was fully rigged.

facts.fact: Wooden panels are painted dark red, blue, tar black, ochre and green; the interior has bare concrete.
facts.quote: Parts of the building are covered in wooden panels painted in dark red, blue, tar black, ochre yellow and dark green. The interior is similarly decorated, with large sections of bare, unpainted concrete, including the entire ceiling.

facts.fact: The ship can be seen from six levels.
facts.quote: Inside the museum the ship can be seen from six levels, from her keel to the very top of the sterncastle.

facts.fact: Previously Vasa was in a temporary structure with views from only two levels.
facts.quote: Visitors could only view the ship from two levels and the maximum distance was only 5 m (17 ft).

facts.fact: Replacement parts on the ship are left unpainted so they stand out from the original wood.
facts.quote: The replacement parts have not been treated or painted and are therefore clearly visible against the original material that has been darkened after three centuries under water.

facts.fact: It is an art museum run by Oberlin College, founded in 1917.
facts.quote: The Allen Memorial Art Museum (AMAM) is an art museum located in Oberlin, Ohio, and run by Oberlin College. Founded in 1917, the collection contains over 15,000 works of art.

facts.fact: Cass Gilbert designed the Italian Renaissance-style building with ironwork by Samuel Yellin.
facts.quote: The collection is housed in an Italian Renaissance-style building designed by Cass Gilbert, incorporating ironwork by Samuel Yellin, and named after its founder, Dr. Dudley Peter Allen (B.A., 1875), a graduate and trustee of Oberlin College and the first husband of Elisabeth Severance Prentiss, whose bequest as Mrs. F. F. Prentiss included parts of her art collection started during her first marriage.

facts.fact: Venturi and Rauch added the 1977 Venturi Wing, an early postmodern work and "decorated shed".
facts.quote: In 1977, the architecture firm Venturi and Rauch (led by husband and wife Robert Venturi and Denise Scott Brown) designed the Venturi Wing, an addition that represents one of the earliest examples of postmodern architecture in the United States; an example of their concept of a "decorated shed".

facts.fact: It is primarily a teaching museum.
facts.quote: The AMAM is primarily a teaching museum and is aimed at the students, faculty and staff of Oberlin College, in addition to the surrounding community.

facts.fact: A central rotunda holds the ancient art wings.
facts.quote: Allen's Central Rotunda, which contains the Egyptian, Greek and Roman art wings

facts.fact: A 2011 retrofit earned LEED Gold.
facts.quote: In 2011, the historic museum underwent a two-year retrofit, after which it was awarded with USGBC LEED Gold certification.

facts.fact: It is a Munich football stadium known for ETFE panels; the first stadium with a full colour-changing exterior.
facts.quote: Widely known for its exterior of inflated ETFE plastic panels, it is the first stadium in the world with a full colour changing exterior.

facts.fact: Herzog & de Meuron are the primary designers; built from October 2002 to May 2005.
facts.quote: The stadium construction began on 21 October 2002 and it was officially opened on 30 May 2005. The primary designers are architects Herzog & de Meuron.

facts.fact: The facade is 2,760 inflated ETFE-foil panels.
facts.quote: The arena facade is constructed of 2,760 ETFE-foil air panels that are kept inflated with dry air to a differential pressure of 3.5 Pa.

facts.fact: Each panel can be lit white, red or blue, in the home team's colours.
facts.quote: Each panel can be independently lit with white, red, or blue light.

facts.fact: The roof has built-in roller blinds for sun protection.
facts.quote: The roof of the stadium has built-in roller blinds which may be drawn back and forth during games to provide protection from the sun.

facts.fact: Entry is from an elevated esplanade above Europe's biggest underground car park.
facts.quote: The stadium is designed so that the main entrance to the stadium would be from an elevated esplanade separated from the parking space consisting of Europe's biggest underground car park.

facts.fact: The police insist on single-colour lighting after Autobahn accidents.
facts.quote: Other colours or multicolour or interchanging lighting schemes are theoretically possible, but the Munich Police strongly insists on using a single-colour lighting scheme due to several car accidents on the nearby A9 Autobahn with drivers being distracted by the changing lights.

facts.fact: The lighting concept was adopted at MetLife Stadium.
facts.quote: Allianz Arena's innovative stadium-facade lighting concept has been subsequently adopted in other recently built venues, like MetLife Stadium in New Jersey, which lights up in blue for the National Football League's Giants and green for the Jets.

facts.fact: Arata Isozaki and Andrea Maffei designed the Milan skyscraper for Allianz's Italian headquarters.
facts.quote: Designed by Japanese architect Arata Isozaki and Italian architect Andrea Maffei, it serves as the headquarters of the Italian subsidiary Allianz SpA.

facts.fact: It is made of eight modules of six floors each.
facts.quote: It is composed by eight modules by six floors each one, with the façade of the module composed by a triple-glass unit slightly curved to outside.

facts.fact: The stacked rounded forms create a slight vibration effect.
facts.quote: The vertical succession of rounded forms creates a feeling of slight vibration of the volume of the building as it rises upward.

facts.fact: The short sides are fully glazed, showing six panoramic lifts.
facts.quote: Elevations of the short sides are fully glazed and show the mechanical series of six panoramic lifts going up and down to the various floors of the building.

facts.fact: The "endless tower" idea is compared to Brâncuși's Endless Column.
facts.quote: The idea of an endless tower can be compared to previous ambitions of other artists, such as Constantin Brâncuși, for example, who in 1937–38 installed one of his endless columns of Târgu Jiu in the park to create repeatable systems indefinitely.

facts.fact: Emporis nominated it third-best skyscraper completed in 2015.
facts.quote: In 2016, Allianz Tower was nominated by Emporis as the third-best skyscraper that was completed in 2015.

facts.fact: Its nickname il Dritto means "the straight one".
facts.quote: Allianz Tower (Italian: Torre Allianz), also known as Isozaki Tower (Italian: Torre Isozaki) and il Dritto ("the straight one"), is a 50-floor, 260-metre-tall (850 ft) skyscraper in Milan, Italy.

facts.fact: It opened in July 2006 in Aomori, Japan.
facts.quote: The Aomori Museum of Art (青森県立美術館, Aomori Kenritsu Bijutsukan) is a museum in Aomori, Japan, opened in July 2006.

facts.fact: Its partially buried structure takes inspiration from the nearby Sannai-Maruyama archaeological site.
facts.quote: It is located near Sannai-Maruyama Site,  which the museum's design takes inspiration from in its partially-buried structure.

facts.fact: It holds more than 120 works by Yoshitomo Nara.
facts.quote: The museum houses more than 120 works from drawings to three-dimensional works by Yoshitomo Nara, a young artist from Aomori Prefecture.

facts.fact: Its Aomori Dog by Nara is its symbol.
facts.quote: The Aomori Dog by Yoshimoto Nara has become the museum's iconic symbol.

facts.fact: It is the largest aquarium in Italy, designed by Renzo Piano for Expo 1992.
facts.quote: The Aquarium of Genoa (Acquario di Genova) is the largest aquarium in Italy and one of the most significant in Europe.

facts.fact: It was designed as part of the urban redevelopment for Expo 1992, the Columbus anniversary.
facts.quote: It is located in the Old Harbour (Porto Antico) area of Genoa, Liguria, and was designed by the architect Renzo Piano as part of the urban redevelopment project created for the Expo 1992, celebrating the 500th anniversary of Christopher Columbus’s voyage to the Americas.

facts.fact: Some say the building looks like a ship ready to sail.
facts.quote: The building, which some say looks like a ship ready to head out to sea, was designed by the Genoese architect Renzo Piano of the Renzo Piano Building Workshop.

facts.fact: Peter Chermayeff and Cambridge Seven Associates designed the interior and first exhibits.
facts.quote: The interior design and initial exhibits for the opening in 1992 were designed by Peter Chermayeff leading a design team at Cambridge Seven Associates.

facts.fact: A 100 m ship was added by walkway in 1998.
facts.quote: In 1998 the aquarium was expanded with the addition of a 100-metre (330 ft) ship connected by walkway to the original building.

facts.fact: It first welcomed the public on 12 October 1993.
facts.quote: The Aquarium of Genoa first welcomed the public on October 12, 1993.

facts.fact: It is a contemporary art museum in a former Tehran brewery from the early 1920s.
facts.quote: Constructed in the early 1920s, Argo Factory was one of the first industrial factories in Iran.

facts.fact: The architects kept the original load-bearing brick walls and inserted new foundations.
facts.quote: The architects retained the original load-bearing brick walls, which expressed the industrial character of the factory.

facts.fact: Five floating concrete roofs are the only new addition to the exterior.
facts.quote: The design taps into the DNA of traditional local metal roofs and rewrites them as five performative floating roofs: each considering an unrepeated lighting atmosphere, for the cultural program underneath it.

facts.fact: The roofs rise above the brick walls, hide mechanical systems and let in natural light.
facts.quote: At the Argo Factory, five elevated concrete roof volumes rise 50 centimeters above the original brick walls, discreetly concealing climate control and mechanical systems within the Roof.

facts.fact: The roofs are inspired by Tehran's halabi metal roofs, and concrete use was necessitated by sanctions.
facts.quote: Inspired by Tehran’s traditional halabi (metal) roofs, the new addition respectfully contrasts the historic structure, while the use of concrete—necessitated by sanctions—reinforces the site's industrial identity.

facts.fact: The footprint grew about 85% to 1,890 m².
facts.quote: The project significantly expanded the building’s original footprint by approximately 85%, increasing the area from 480 m² to 1,890 m².

facts.fact: Pejman Foundation reconstructed it in 2016.
facts.quote: In 2016, Pejman Foundation acquired and reconstructed the factory.

facts.fact: Albert Chase McArthur designed it; it opened 23 February 1929.
facts.quote: Designed by Albert Chase McArthur, it opened on February 23, 1929, as part of the Biltmore Hotel chain.

facts.fact: Wright consulted on the "Textile Block" construction, so the design is often misattributed to him.
facts.quote: The Arizona Biltmore's architect of record is Albert Chase McArthur (brother of the hotel owners), yet the design is often mistakenly attributed to Frank Lloyd Wright. This is due to Wright's on-site consulting for four months in 1928 relating to the "Textile Block" construction used in the hotel.

facts.fact: The block system became a signature of the hotel's appearance.
facts.quote: Albert McArthur had been a draftsman for Wright and specifically asked him to assist with implementing the textile block system, which became a signature element of the hotel's appearance.

facts.fact: Drawings in the ASU archives and a 1929 Architectural Record article confirm McArthur as architect.
facts.quote: McArthur is indisputably the architect, as original linen drawings of the hotel in the Arizona State University Library archives attest, as does a 1929 feature article in Architectural Record magazine.

facts.fact: The lobby shows a strong imprint of Wright's unit block design.
facts.quote: The hotel has similarities to several Wright buildings, especially in the main lobby, owing to a strong imprint of the unit block design that Wright had utilized on four residential buildings in the Los Angeles area six years earlier.

facts.fact: A stained glass window Wright designed for a 1926 magazine cover is among Wright influences at the property.
facts.quote: This includes a stained glass window design entitled "Saguaro Forms and Cactus Flowers" that Wright designed as a magazine cover for Liberty Magazine in 1926.

facts.fact: Kengo Kuma won a competition to design it; it opened 20 April 2012.
facts.quote: By 2008, the building had deteriorated and a competition was held to design a new building, with Kengo Kuma being the winner.

facts.fact: It is a stack of separate wooden buildings piled at different angles.
facts.quote: The steel-based building is essentially "a stack of separate wooden buildings that have been piled up on top of each other at different angles", according to architecture media company Architizer.

facts.fact: The exterior is mostly Japanese cedar and glass, treated to be fireproof.
facts.quote: The exterior focuses mostly on wood (mainly Japanese cedar) and glass, which reflects traditional Japanese architecture while adding a contemporary twist.

facts.fact: Height was reduced from 41.3 m to 38.9 m after concerns about the scenery.
facts.quote: The center was originally going to be 41.3 m (135 ft) tall, but the city's assembly raised concerns that it could disrupt the scenery around the building. Because of this, its height was reduced to 38.9 m (128 ft).

facts.fact: Kuma was reminded of Edo-period nagaya houses and stacked modern versions of them.
facts.quote: When designing the center, Kuma was reminded of the traditional nagaya houses from Tokyo's Edo period, stacking a more modern version of these dwellings on top of each other, trying to create an unbalanced void in between each of the floors.

facts.fact: The slanted roofs leave voids between floors used for equipment.
facts.quote: Kuma used these voids to store equipment and technical facilities, saying "We are too used to the idea that the floors have to be flat, but I hope I was able to inspire people to re-think the relationships of buildings and floors."

facts.fact: The sixth floor has a terraced theatre under the slanted roof.
facts.quote: The first and second floors have an atrium, while the sixth floor takes advantage of the slanted roof to create a terraced floor that functions as a theater.

facts.fact: It won a 2012 Good Design Award.
facts.quote: It was a recipient of the 2012 Good Design Award.

facts.fact: Renzo Piano designed the museum's two new buildings; it opened 29 September 2012.
facts.quote: The new museum was designed by the architect Renzo Piano and opened on 29 September 2012

facts.fact: It moved to Tjuvholmen in 2012.
facts.quote: In 2012 the museum moved to two new buildings designed by Renzo Piano in Tjuvholmen.

facts.fact: The sculpture park around it was also by Piano.
facts.quote: The museum is situated in the Tjuvholmen skulpturpark, also designed by Renzo Piano.

facts.fact: The museum is privately owned and was founded in 1993.
facts.quote: The Astrup Fearnley Museum (Norwegian: Astrup Fearnley Museet) is a  privately owned contemporary art museum in Oslo in Norway. It was founded and opened to the public in 1993.

facts.fact: The original building is French Renaissance style in brick and plaster, completed 1887.
facts.quote: It is constructed of brick and plaster in an early French Renaissance style and was completed in 1887, with an extension built in 1916.

facts.fact: FJMT with Archimedia designed the extension, finished in 2011.
facts.quote: The expansion design by Australian architecture firm FJMT in partnership with Auckland-based Archimedia  increased exhibition space by 50%, for up to 900 artworks,  and provided dedicated education, child and family spaces.

facts.fact: The extension needed land from Albert Park and drew criticism.
facts.quote: In the late 2000s, a major extension was mooted, which drew substantial criticism from some quarters due to its cost, design and the fact that land from Albert Park would be required.

facts.fact: It was established in 1888 as New Zealand's first permanent art gallery.
facts.quote: Set below the hilltop Albert Park in the central-city area of Auckland, the gallery was established in 1888 as the first permanent art gallery in New Zealand.

facts.fact: It originally housed a public library too.
facts.quote: The building originally housed both the Auckland Art Gallery and the Auckland public library, and opened with collections donated by benefactors Governor Sir George Grey and James Tannock Mackelvie.

facts.fact: H. H. Richardson designed it as a Harvard Law School classroom building.
facts.quote: Austin Hall is a classroom building of the Harvard Law School designed by noted American architect H. H. Richardson.

facts.fact: It was the first building purpose-built for an American law school.
facts.quote: The first building purposely built for an American law school, it was also the first dedicated home of Harvard Law School.

facts.fact: It is Romanesque Revival, built 1882–1884, with a T-shaped plan.
facts.quote: The hall was built 1882–1884 in Romanesque Revival style. Single-story wings flank a heavy, two-story central mass, with the reading room extending rearwards to form an overall T shape.

facts.fact: A deep Romanesque triple arch frames the entry with an asymmetric stair tower.
facts.quote: A central entryway framed with Romanesque triple arch is set deep within the building's flat front facade, with an asymmetric stairway tower protruding forwards to its right.

facts.fact: Longmeadow sandstone forms checkerboard polychrome patterns, with pale Ohio sandstone arches.
facts.quote: The building is faced with Longmeadow sandstone in striking polychrome patterns, the light stones forming checkerboards within dark, reddish walls.

facts.fact: Three large classrooms suit the Socratic-method curriculum; the layout has been imitated.
facts.quote: Austin Hall's first floor contains three large classrooms; these were designed to complement the new law school curriculum that was being implemented at the time by Dean Christopher Columbus Langdell, including large core classes employing the Socratic method.

facts.fact: The reading room has an ornamented fireplace and carved tie beams.
facts.quote: The reading room's interior has been judged particularly fine for its ornamented fireplace and tie beams carved with the heads of dragons and boars.

facts.fact: It was Victor Horta's first town house, built 1893 in Brussels.
facts.quote: This house, built in 1893, was the first designed by Victor Horta in Art Nouveau style, and represents an essential step in the evolution of the Belgian architect.

facts.fact: Budget limits led the family to want a simple home, dropping custom details.
facts.quote: Due to budget restrictions, the family wanted a simple but comfortable home. For this reason, many custom made details, which Horta designed himself in most of the other town houses he built, were abolished.

facts.fact: Art Nouveau features include iron pillars, sgraffito, stained glass, mosaics and natural light.
facts.quote: All typical Art Nouveau characteristics are already present in this early work of Horta: fine iron pillars and columns of the façade, sgraffito, stained glass, mosaics, and importance of natural light and decorative elements of floral inspiration.

facts.fact: The decorative scheme made no reference to historical styles, but the plan stayed traditional.
facts.quote: This dwelling was already innovative for its application of a novel Art Nouveau decorative scheme that did not include references to other historical styles. However, the floor plan and spatial composition of the Autrique House remained rather traditional.

facts.fact: The middle room of the three-room suite was gloomy.
facts.quote: From the three-room suite, only the first and the last had windows, and so the middle room, used mostly as a dining room, was rather gloomy.

facts.fact: It was restored and opened to the public after being bought in the 1990s.
facts.quote: In the 1990s, it was bought by the municipality of Schaerbeek. It was thoroughly renovated and is now opened to the public.

facts.fact: Uglješa Bogunović and Slobodan Janjić designed it with engineer Milan Krstić.
facts.quote: The tower was designed by architects Uglješa Bogunović and Slobodan Janjić, and engineer Milan Krstić.

facts.fact: The original tower was finished in 1965, destroyed in 1999, and reopened in 2010.
facts.quote: The original tower was finished in 1965, but was destroyed on 29 April 1999, during the NATO bombing of Yugoslavia.

facts.fact: It was the only tower with an equilateral triangle cross-section.
facts.quote: It was the only tower in the world to have an equilateral triangle as its cross section, and one of very few towers not perched directly into the ground, but standing on its legs.

facts.fact: Its legs formed a tripod echoing the Serbian tronožac stool.
facts.quote: The legs formed a tripod, the symbol of Serbian tripod chair (tronožac).

facts.fact: An enclosed observation deck sat between 102 m and 135 m.
facts.quote: Between 102 m (335 ft) and 135 m (443 ft), there was an enclosed observation deck, entered at 122 m (400 ft) and reached via two quick elevators.

facts.fact: It was finished without any worker deaths or injuries.
facts.quote: The project, which was of high risk, was finished without any worker injuries or deaths, which was unusual for a project of its size.

facts.fact: Construction of the replacement began in December 2006.
facts.quote: The tower's reconstruction commenced on 21 December 2006.

facts.fact: It is a mausoleum and museum in Hamadan with a 28 m spindle-shaped tower inspired by Kavus Tower.
facts.quote: Dedicated to the Persian polymath Avicenna, the complex includes a library, a small museum, and a spindle-shaped 28-metre-high (92 ft) tower inspired by the Ziyarid-era Kavus Tower.

facts.fact: Houshang Seyhoun won the competition and trained in France.
facts.quote: Houshang Seyhoun won competitions for the mausoleums of Ferdowsi and Avicenna before heading to France.

facts.fact: It was dedicated in May 1954 for the philosopher's millennial birth anniversary.
facts.quote: The mausoleum was eventually dedicated in a grand ceremony in May 1954, on the occasion of the philosopher's millennial birth anniversary, and the avenue running in front of it was also renamed in honor of Avicenna.

facts.fact: It was added to Iran's National Heritage List in 1997.
facts.quote: The mausoleum and museum complex was added to the Iran National Heritage List on 11 May 1997 and is administered by the Cultural Heritage, Handicrafts and Tourism Organization of Iran.

facts.fact: The square kept its name after 1979 because Khomeini admired Avicenna.
facts.quote: As the monument was constructed by the Pahlavi government, it was consequently in danger of being defaced, but as Khomeini was an admirer of Avicenna, the square was not renamed after the 1979 Revolution.

facts.fact: It is a private museum in Makati run by the Ayala Foundation.
facts.quote: The Ayala Museum is a museum in Makati, Metro Manila, Philippines. It is run privately by the Ayala Foundation and houses archaeological, ethnographic, historical, fine arts, numismatics, and ecclesiastical exhibits.

facts.fact: The new building is six storeys of granite, steel and glass.
facts.quote: The museum moved to a new six-story building made from granite, steel and glass,  which was designed by Leandro V. Locsin Partners, led by Leandro Y. Locsin Jr., the son of the architect that designed the old Ayala Museum.

facts.fact: It was dedicated on 28 September 2004 on the site of the original museum.
facts.quote: It was formally dedicated at the 170th anniversary of the Ayala Corporation on September 28, 2004, and stands on the same site of the original Ayala Museum.

facts.fact: Leandro Locsin designed the old building, whose demolition drew heritage criticism.
facts.quote: The old building that hosted the old Ayala Museum was demolished which met some criticism from heritage conservationists.

facts.fact: The museum was established in April 1967.
facts.quote: Envisioned during the 1950s by Philippine abstract painter Fernando M. Zobel, as a museum of Philippine history and iconography, the Ayala Museum was established in April 1967 as a project of the Filipinas Foundation, now known as the Ayala Foundation.

facts.fact: It reopened on 4 December 2021 after renovation.
facts.quote: The museum was reopened on December 4, 2021, after a two-year renovation.

facts.fact: It is a Baháʼí House of Worship dedicated in 1961, the "mother Temple of Africa".
facts.quote: The Kampala Baháʼí Temple is a Baháʼí House of Worship, known to Baháʼís as the "mother Temple of Africa" and located on the outskirts of Kampala, Uganda.

facts.fact: It was the tallest building in East Africa when built.
facts.quote: It was dedicated in 1961, making it the world's third Baháʼí House of Worship to be completed, and at that time it was the tallest building in East Africa.

facts.fact: Charles Mason Remey prepared the approved design in Haifa.
facts.quote: Following an initial design which had been rejected, a new design was prepared in Haifa by the Charles Mason Remey, under the direction of Shoghi Effendi, which received approval in August 1956.

facts.fact: It was built after persecution in Iran made the Tehran plan impossible.
facts.quote: However, an outbreak of persecution of Baháʼís in Iran in 1955 made this plan impossible, so he announced that two other Houses of Worship would be built, in Kampala, Uganda, and Sydney, Australia.

facts.fact: The dome is Italian mosaic tile and the lower roof Belgian tile.
facts.quote: The temple's dome is built out of fixed mosaic tiles from Italy, whereas the tiles of the lower roof are from Belgium.

facts.fact: Windows are German coloured glass; timber and stone are Ugandan.
facts.quote: The wall panels contain windows of green, pale blue, and amber colored glass of German origin. Both the timber used for making the doors and benches and the stone used for the walls of the temple are from within Uganda itself.

facts.fact: The foundation goes 3 metres deep as protection against earthquakes.
facts.quote: As a protection against earthquakes that can occur in the region, the temple has a foundation that goes 3 metres beneath the ground.

facts.fact: George Chakhava and Zurab Jalaghania designed it for the Georgian SSR highway ministry; finished 1975.
facts.quote: It was designed by architects George Chakhava and Zurab Jalaghania  for the Ministry of Highway Construction of the Georgian SSR and finished in 1975.

facts.fact: Chakhava was both the client and lead architect and could choose the site.
facts.quote: George Chakhava was Georgia's Deputy Minister of Highway Construction in the 1970s. Therefore, he was both the client and the lead architect of this project. He could choose the site location best suited for the design himself.

facts.fact: The design uses the "Space City method", covering less ground and leaving space below for nature.
facts.quote: The idea is to use and cover less ground and give the space below the building back to nature.

facts.fact: The cores are like trunks and the horizontal parts like crowns.
facts.quote: The architect's reference was a forest: the cores are like the trunk, the horizontal parts the crowns.

facts.fact: It echoes El Lissitzky's horizontal skyscrapers of 1924.
facts.quote: The architect El Lissitzky designed with his horizontal skyscrapers (Wolkenbügel) 1924 a structure that looks very similar.

facts.fact: Fair-faced concrete and sharp geometry mean it can be seen as Brutalist.
facts.quote: Based on the use of fairfaced concrete and the sharp, geometrical volumes, the building can also be considered as part of the Brutalism movement.

facts.fact: The Bank of Georgia bought it in 2007 and it gained monument status.
facts.quote: In 2007 the building was acquired by the Bank of Georgia. In the same year it was also conferred an Immovable Monument status under the National Monuments Acts.

facts.fact: It is Yale's rare book library, designed by Gordon Bunshaft of SOM and completed in 1963.
facts.quote: Situated on Yale University's Hewitt Quadrangle, the building was designed by Gordon Bunshaft of Skidmore, Owings & Merrill and completed in 1963.

facts.fact: A glass tower of book stacks sits within a windowless facade on four corner piers.
facts.quote: Its six-story above-ground glass-enclosed tower of book stacks is encased by a windowless façade, supported by four monolithic piers at the corners of the building.

facts.fact: The facade is translucent veined marble and granite, 1.25 inches thick, letting in amber light.
facts.quote: The marble was quarried from Danby, Vermont, and milled to a thickness of 1.25 inches (32 mm) in order to allow filtered daylight to permeate the interior in a subtle golden amber glow.

facts.fact: Bunshaft recalled alabaster in a Renaissance-type palace in Istanbul as the inspiration.

facts.fact: Marble panels are framed by a hexagonal granite grid on a steel frame.

facts.fact: Its outside dimensions have 1:2:3 proportions.
facts.quote: The outside dimensions have Platonic mathematical proportions of 1:2:3 (height: width: length).

facts.fact: A mezzanine surrounds the glass stack tower and shows a Gutenberg Bible.
facts.quote: An elevated public exhibition mezzanine surrounds the glass stack tower, and displays among other things, one of the 48 extant copies of the Gutenberg Bible.

facts.fact: It is International Style and called a "jewel box".
facts.quote: The Beinecke Library is an International Style building.

facts.fact: Charles Correa designed this multi-arts complex in Bhopal.
facts.quote: Bharat Bhavan is an autonomous multi-arts complex and museum in Bhopal, India, established and funded by the Government of Madhya Pradesh. The architect of the Bharat Bhavan is Charles Correa.

facts.fact: It opened in 1982 facing the Upper Lake.
facts.quote: Opened in 1982, facing the Upper Lake, Bhopal, it houses multiple art galleries, a graphic printing workshop, a ceramics workshop, an open-air amphitheatre, a studio theatre, an auditorium, a museum of tribal & folk art, and libraries of Indian poetry, classical music & folk music.

facts.fact: Indira Gandhi inaugurated it on 13 February 1982.
facts.quote: The institution was inaugurated on 13 February 1982  by then Prime Minister, Indira Gandhi.

facts.fact: It is run by an autonomous trust and funded by Madhya Pradesh.
facts.quote: It was established and funded by the Department of Culture, Government of Madhya Pradesh,  though it is run by an autonomous 12-member Bharat Bhavan Trust.

facts.fact: Steven Holl won a 1999 international competition for the addition.
facts.quote: Architect Steven Holl won an international competition in 1999 for the design of the addition.

facts.fact: Holl and Chris McVoy designed five glass pavilions ("lenses") above an underground building.
facts.quote: Holl's concept, conceived and realized with Design Partner Chris McVoy, was to build five glass pavilions to the east of the original building which they call lenses. The lenses top a 165,000-square-foot (15,300 m ) underground building known as the Bloch Building.

facts.fact: It houses contemporary, African and photography galleries, a cafe, a library and the Noguchi Sculpture Court.
facts.quote: The Bloch building houses the museum's contemporary, African, photography, and special exhibitions galleries as well a new cafe, the museum's Spencer Art Reference Library, and the Isamu Noguchi Sculpture Court.

facts.fact: Other entrants proposed north-side additions; Holl placed his east, perpendicular, to engage the sculpture garden.
facts.quote: Instead Holl and McVoy proposed placing the addition on the east side perpendicular to the main building. Their aim was to engage the museum's iconic sculpture garden to fuse the experience of art, architecture and landscape.

facts.fact: It opened 9 June 2007.
facts.quote: The addition cost approximately $95 million and opened June 9, 2007.

facts.fact: Time ranked it number one on a 2007 list of architectural marvels.
facts.quote: In 2007, Time magazine ranked the museum's new Bloch Building number one on its list of "The 10 Best (New and Upcoming) Architectural Marvels" which considered candidates from around the globe.

facts.fact: The plan was controversial during construction but reviews were generally positive.
facts.quote: During construction, Holl's plan met with considerable controversy.

facts.fact: The original 1933 building is Beaux-Arts by Wight and Wight.
facts.quote: The building was designed by prominent Kansas City architects Wight and Wight, who also designed the approaches to the Liberty Memorial and the Kansas governor's mansion, Cedar Crest.

facts.fact: It is two residential towers in Milan's Porta Nuova with plants on the facades.
facts.quote: The Bosco Verticale (Vertical Forest) is a complex of two residential skyscrapers designed by Boeri Studio (Stefano Boeri, Gianandrea Barreca, and Giovanni La Varra) and located in the Porta Nuova district of Milan, Italy.

facts.fact: Over ninety plant species, including trees and shrubs, grow on the facades.
facts.quote: The distinctive feature of the skyscrapers, both inaugurated in 2014, is the presence of over ninety plant species, including tall shrubs and trees, distributed on the facades.

facts.fact: Boeri reacted against glass-clad "mineral cities" after a visit to Dubai.
facts.quote: During a visit to the metropolis of Dubai in the United Arab Emirates, the architect had the impression of being in a "mineral city, made up of dozens of new towers and skyscrapers, all clad in glass or ceramics or metal, all reflecting sunlight and therefore generating heat in the air and especially on the ground inhabited by pedestrians."

facts.fact: Boeri says it was inspired by Calvino's The Baron in the Trees.
facts.quote: According to Boeri, the building was inspired by Italo Calvino's 1957 novel The Baron in the Trees, in which the protagonist decides to abandon the ground and live in the trees for the rest of his life.

facts.fact: Together the towers have 800 trees, 5,000 shrubs and 1,500 perennials.
facts.quote: The project was named Bosco Verticale, or in English "Vertical Forest", because together the towers have 800 trees, 5,000 shrubs and 1,500 perennial plants, which help mitigate smog and produce oxygen.

facts.fact: The vegetation shades interiors, blocks wind, and cuts noise and dust.
facts.quote: It is also used to moderate temperatures in the buildings in the winter and summer, by shading the interiors from the sun and blocking harsh winds. The vegetation also protects the interior spaces from noise pollution and dust from street-level traffic.

facts.fact: It won the International Highrise Award in 2014.
facts.quote: In addition to the International Highrise Award in 2014, it was acknowledged by the Council on Tall Buildings and Urban Habitat as the "most beautiful and innovative skyscraper in the world" in 2015 and as one of the "fifty most iconic skyscrapers in the world" in 2019.

facts.fact: Sir Albert Richardson designed it as a late example of modern classicism on a bomb site.
facts.quote: A late example of modern classicism, it was designed  by Sir Albert Richardson and constructed on a cleared bomb site southeast of St Paul's Cathedral.

facts.fact: It is clad in pink Hollington sandstone, a nod to the Financial Times's pink paper.
facts.quote: The building was clad in pink sandstone from Hollington, Staffordshire, as an allusion to the characteristic pink colour of the newspaper, with red bricks and bronze windows, contrasting with the verdigris of the copper roof.

facts.fact: An astronomical clock above the Cannon Street entrance has Churchill's face at the centre.
facts.quote: Above the entrance on Cannon Street is an astronomical clock, designed by Frank Dobson and Philip Bentham and made by Thwaites & Reed.

facts.fact: It was among the first post-war English buildings to be listed, in 1987.
facts.quote: It became a Grade II listed building in 1987 – the first building built in England after the Second World War to become listed – and was upgraded to Grade II* in 2013.

facts.fact: Michael Hopkins and Partners redesigned the central part between 1988 and 1992.
facts.quote: The central part of the building was redesigned by Michael Hopkins and Partners between 1988 and 1992.

facts.fact: The new centre is glass and gunmetal with oriel windows inspired by Oriel Chambers.
facts.quote: The altered building retained the old ranges to the north and south, but replaced the central printing hall with a new glass and structural gunmetal structure on a Hollington sandstone plinth, with boxy oriel windows inspired by Oriel Chambers in Liverpool, constructed in 1864.

facts.fact: The Financial Times moved back in 2019.
facts.quote: After refurbishments by John Robertson Architects, the Financial Times moved back into Bracken House in spring 2019.

facts.fact: Colin St John Wilson designed it with his wife MJ Long.
facts.quote: The new library was designed by the architect Colin St John Wilson  in collaboration with his wife MJ Long.

facts.fact: It was the largest public building built in the UK in the 20th century.
facts.quote: It was the largest public building constructed in the United Kingdom in the 20th century.

facts.fact: A large piazza on Euston Road holds sculptures by Paolozzi and Gormley.
facts.quote: Facing Euston Road is a large piazza that includes pieces of public art, such as large sculptures by Eduardo Paolozzi (a bronze statue based on William Blake's study of Isaac Newton) and Antony Gormley.

facts.fact: A six-storey glass tower, inspired by one at the Beinecke Library, holds the King's Library.
facts.quote: A central six-storey glass tower inspired by a similar structure in the Beinecke Library, contains the King's Library with 65,000 printed volumes along with other pamphlets, manuscripts and maps collected by King George III between 1763 and 1820.

facts.fact: It stands next to St Pancras station and opened on 25 June 1998.
facts.quote: The Library's purpose-built building stands next to St Pancras station in London. It was officially opened by Elizabeth II on 25 June 1998, and is classified as a Grade I listed building "of exceptional interest" for its architecture and history.

facts.fact: Eleven new reading rooms opened as stock moved from the old Round Reading Room.
facts.quote: Before the end of that year the first of eleven new reading rooms had opened and the moving of stock was continuing.

facts.fact: It was Grade I listed on 1 August 2015.
facts.quote: The Euston Road building was Grade I listed on 1 August 2015.

facts.fact: It is a long unbroken block of 620 maisonettes in Newcastle designed by Ralph Erskine.
facts.quote: The Byker Wall is a long, unbroken block of 620 maisonettes in the Byker district of Newcastle upon Tyne, England. They were designed by Ralph Erskine and constructed in the 1970s.

facts.fact: It replaced Victorian slum terraces condemned in 1953.
facts.quote: The Wall, along with the low-rise dwellings built to its south, replaced Victorian slum terraced housing. There were nearly 1200 houses on the site at Byker. They had been condemned as unfit for human habitation in 1953, and demolition began in 1966.

facts.fact: Erskine opened a site office to build trust with residents.
facts.quote: The architects opened an office on site to develop communication and trust between the existing residents.

facts.fact: The wall shields the estate from a motorway that was never built.
facts.quote: The new high-rise block was designed to shield the site from an intended motorway, which was never built.

facts.fact: Cheap concrete, brick and timber, bright colours and brick bands marking floors were used.
facts.quote: Construction materials for Byker Wall were relatively cheap, concrete, brick and timber. Surfaces were treated with bright colours, while brick bandings were used on the 'Wall' to indicate floor levels.

facts.fact: Its "Functionalist Romantic" styling broke with Brutalist high-rise orthodoxy.
facts.quote: Its Functionalist Romantic styling with textured, complex facades, colourful brick, wood and plastic panels, attention to context, and relatively low-rise construction represented a major break with the Brutalist high-rise architectural orthodoxy of the time.

facts.fact: Design began in 1968 and construction ran 1969–1982.
facts.quote: Design began in 1968  and construction took place between 1969 and 1982.

facts.fact: Fewer than 20% of the original residents were rehoused there.
facts.quote: Following completion, fewer than 20% of the original local residents were housed at Byker Wall.

facts.fact: It is an Edwardian building of 1905 in honey-coloured limestone imported from Bath.

facts.fact: A public competition was won by Harry Austin Reid and Frederick George Green.
facts.quote: The winning architects were Messrs Harry Austin Reid and Frederick George Green, with the contractors being Messrs T. Howard and F. G. Scott.

facts.fact: Much of the material and fittings were imported from Europe.

facts.fact: A city hall had been mooted in 1887 for Queen Victoria's Golden Jubilee.

facts.fact: The auditorium organ has 3,165 pipes.
facts.quote: There are altogether 3165 pipes varying from 32 feet (10 metres) to  3⁄4 inch (19 millimetres).

facts.fact: The tower has a turret clock chiming Westminster quarters.

facts.fact: It is Christchurch's transitional cathedral, built after the 2011 earthquake.
