facts.fact: Shigeru Ban designed it with Warren and Mahoney; it opened in August 2013.
facts.quote: The Cardboard Cathedral was designed by the Japanese architect Shigeru Ban in association with Warren and Mahoney and opened in August 2013.

facts.fact: The nickname comes from over 90 large cardboard tubes in the walls and roof.
facts.quote: The church gets its nickname from the use of over 90 large cardboard tubes for its walls and roof.

facts.fact: Ban designed it pro bono and is called a "disaster architect".
facts.quote: Ban, who is characterised as a "disaster architect", designed the building pro bono,  in collaboration with Christchurch architecture firm Warren and Mahoney.

facts.fact: It is A-frame in style, rising 24 metres, with tubes atop shipping containers.
facts.quote: A-frame in style, rising 24 metres (79 ft), it incorporated 86 cardboard tubes of 500 kilograms (1,100 lb) each atop 6 metres (20 ft) long containers.

facts.fact: It stands on the site of the demolished St John the Baptist Church.
facts.quote: It was originally the site of St John the Baptist Church, the first church built in permanent materials by Anglicans in Christchurch, which was demolished after the 2011 Christchurch earthquake.

facts.fact: It combines cardboard, wood and glass.

facts.fact: The archdiocese added Pier Luigi Nervi and Pietro Belluschi to the design team after early options drew negative feedback.
facts.quote: However, the options that the architects originally presented received negative feedback. The archdiocese then added the Italian architect Pier Luigi Nervi and the American architect Pietro Belluschi to the design team.

facts.fact: The brief asked for a structure where crowds could surround the altar.
facts.quote: a cathedral that would accommodate large numbers of people; one that would enable even large crowds to surround the altar; and a structure that would be a statement that God is present in beauty in the earthly city.

facts.fact: The saddle roof is eight hyperbolic paraboloid segments, square at the base and cross-shaped at the top.

facts.fact: The upper portion is precast concrete.
facts.quote: Precast concrete work, the entire top portion of the building, was constructed by Terracon and the DiRegolo Family of Hayward, California.

facts.fact: It measures 255 feet square and 190 feet high, crowned by a golden cross.
facts.quote: Measuring 255 feet (78 m) square, Saint Mary's Cathedral is 190 feet (58 m) high and is crowned with a 55 feet (17 m) golden cross.

facts.fact: Many Catholics disliked it, with nicknames such as "Our Lady of Maytag".
facts.quote: Some called it "Our Lady of Perpetual Agitation" or "Our Lady of Maytag" because the roof (designed to look like a conquistador's helmet) resembled the agitator in a washing machine.

facts.fact: The AIA's San Francisco chapter listed it among the city's top 25 buildings in 2007.
facts.quote: Saint Mary's Cathedral was selected in 2007 by the local chapter of the American Institute of Architects for a list of San Francisco's top 25 buildings.

facts.fact: It is a brutalist building by João Filgueiras Lima nicknamed the "Balance Building".
facts.quote: The Centro de Exposições do Centro Administrativo da Bahia, known as the "Prédio da Balança", "Balance Building" is a brutalist building by João Filgueiras Lima at the Centro Administrativo da Bahia [pt] in Bahia, Brazil.

facts.fact: It was designed in 1974 and marks the entrance to the administrative centre.

facts.fact: A concrete box is suspended by cables from two identical towers.

facts.fact: The exhibition hall has a pyramidal ceiling with a skylight and the amphitheater inverts that space.

facts.fact: To show it was stable, Lima and Kertész stood under it as supports were removed.
facts.quote: To demonstrate it was stable, Lima and Kertész stood underneath as the construction supports were removed.

facts.fact: It was in disrepair by 2021, with emergency shoring in 2024.
facts.quote: As of 2021, the building was in disrepair and no longer used. Renovations have been needed for decades.

facts.fact: Minoru Yamasaki designed two 44-storey twin towers for Alcoa, completed 1975.

facts.fact: They have an unusual triangular footprint.

facts.quote: They are the tallest buildings in California outside Downtown Los Angeles and San Francisco.

facts.fact: It is a Catholic chapel built 1954–1956 into the red rock buttes of Sedona.

facts.quote: It was inspired and commissioned by local rancher and sculptor Marguerite Brunswig Staude, and was designed by August K. Strotz of the firm of Anshen & Allen, with Richard Hein of the firm as the project architect.

facts.fact: A 90 ft iron cross on the wall is both symbol and structure.

facts.fact: Walls are 1-foot reinforced concrete, sandblasted to show the aggregate.
facts.quote: The walls and cross are constructed with reinforced coarse-aggregate concrete, 1 foot (0.3 m) in thickness. Inside and out, the walls were sandblasted to unveil the textured aggregate.

facts.fact: Smoky-grey glass at the ends reduces glare.

facts.fact: It was built in 18 months and moved 25 tons of rock without dynamite.

facts.fact: The AIA gave it an Award of Honor in 1957.

facts.fact: The Mother Church of 1894 and 1906 extension stand with it.

facts.fact: It received the Twenty-five Year Award.
facts.quote: It has also received numerous awards, including the Twenty-five Year Award for architectural excellence.

facts.fact: Roche-Dinkeloo added Deere West in 1978, with offices around a glass-roofed atrium.
facts.quote: Roche-Dinkeloo was hired in 1975 to design Deere West, which opened in 1978.

facts.fact: It is a high-rise federal office building and courthouse in Albuquerque, completed in 1965.
facts.quote: The Dennis Chavez Federal Building is a high-rise federal office building and courthouse located at 500 Gold Avenue SW in Downtown Albuquerque, New Mexico. It was completed in 1965

facts.fact: It was renamed for Senator Dennis Chavez in 1976.
facts.quote: Originally known simply as the U.S. Courthouse and Federal Office Building, the building was renamed in honor of longtime U.S. Senator Dennis Chavez in 1976.

facts.fact: An Albuquerque firm, Flatow, Moore, Bryan, and Fairburn, designed it.
facts.quote: The Dennis Chavez Building was designed by the Albuquerque firm of Flatow, Moore, Bryan, and Fairburn, which had previously been responsible for other local highrises like the Simms Building and Bank of the West Tower.

facts.fact: It has a steel frame, polished granite facing and New Mexico marble in the lobby.
facts.quote: The steel-framed building is faced with polished granite, with New Mexico marble used in the ground floor lobby.

facts.fact: It has 13 floors above ground.
facts.quote: It is 197 feet (60 m) in height and has 13 above-ground floors with a basement and underground parking garage.

facts.fact: It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 2023.
facts.quote: The building was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 2023.

facts.fact: It housed Design Research, a store founded in 1953 that introduced the lifestyle store.
facts.quote: Design Research (abbreviated and trademarked as D/R) was a retail store founded in 1953 by Ben Thompson in Cambridge, Massachusetts, and which introduced the concept of lifestyle store.

facts.fact: Benjamin Thompson and Associates designed the 1969 building at 48 Brattle Street, Harvard Square.
facts.quote: In 1969, Thompson moved the original Cambridge store to a revolutionary new 24,000-square-foot (2,200 m ) building designed by his firm, Benjamin Thompson and Associates, at 48 Brattle Street in Harvard Square, on a block that came to be known as "Architects' Corner".

facts.fact: It has five storeys of concrete slabs on interior columns, enclosed by frameless tempered glass.
facts.quote: The 5-story building consists of flat concrete slabs supported by interior columns, and enclosed by frameless tempered glass walls.

facts.fact: Butted glass without frames or mullions was unprecedented.
facts.quote: The use of butted glass with no frame or mullions was unprecedented, and "allowed D/R to be a building almost 'without architecture'".

facts.fact: It was conceived as a glass showcase faceted like a diamond.
facts.quote: is conceived as a five-story glass showcase, faceted like the surface of a diamond.

facts.fact: Reviews praised it as pointing to glass building that could warm the city.
facts.quote: It immediately received favorable reviews: "points the way to a method of glass building that could create a warmer city, adding color and light and optimism to the life of the streets".

facts.fact: The store carried furniture by designers such as Breuer, Wegner, Aalto and Colombo.
facts.quote: It carried furnishings by such designers as Marcel Breuer, Hans Wegner, Alvar Aalto, and Joe Colombo.
